To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
human populations are associated with declines in reef-building corals and increases in fleshy non-calcifying organisms on Pacific reefs.
human populations have a significant impact on the structure of coral reef communities, and that this impact is widespread across the Pacific.

1) human impacts have resulted in a reduction in the relative abundance of reef-building organisms across the central Pacific; 2) the relative abundances of fleshy macroalgal species have increased on inhabited reefs; and 3) coral cover has declined on inhabited reefs, but has remained relatively high on uninhabited reefs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the health of the coral reef ecosystem.
understanding the effects of human populations on coral reefs and how this is reflected in the structure and function of benthic communities.
the effects of human populations on the health and function of coral reefs, and the implications of our findings for the conservation and management of coral reefs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
coral reefs are not in good health, and that the human population is the cause.
the health of coral reefs is declining across the central Pacific, and the presence of humans is a significant driver of these changes.
human habitation is associated with a reduction in the relative abundance of reef builders and a shift towards fleshy organisms on reefs in the Pacific.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
human populations are associated with declines in the abundance and diversity of calcifying organisms, while fleshy macrophytes and non-calcifiers are more abundant on inhabited islands.
human impacts are widespread across the central Pacific and that the health of coral reefs is being compromised by the activities of humans.
human populations are associated with declines in calcifying benthos and increases in the abundance of fleshy non-calcifying benthos.
The main takeaway from our work is that
coral reefs are not static and the health of reef communities can change rapidly in the presence of human activities.
coral reef community assessments that focus on coral and macroalgae alone may be missing important information on the overall structure and function of these systems.
human populations can have large effects on the structure of coral reef communities and these effects may be widespread across the central Pacific.
